new:
In this experiment, the people were placing a higher value on an object they were given.

When they were given the mug, they valued it as worth more than $5. When they were considering purchasing it, they valued it as worth $5 max.

This answer is saying that people usually place too low a value in objects they've been given.

That points the wrong way. If people tend to undervalue objects they've been given, we'd expect the participants to value their free mug lower, not hold out for more than $5. So this answer does nothing to resolve the discrepancy; if anything, it deepens it.

new:
After reading the argument on a Parallel question, we have to decide whether we think it would be more effective to make an Algebra Recipe for the argument or to just boil it down to a Principle or Reasoning Pattern. My general rule of thumb is that if there's conditional logic or quantifiers or Overlapping Ideas, then I'll go for Algebra. The first two premises are quantified/conditional logic (no / every). And there are Overlapping Ideas: Carriage Books, nonfiction book, profit, publish are all mentioned at least twice. So if we assign them some variables, we can look at the logic.
```
Premise 1: No X's from Thing A have ever been Y.
  For Thing A (all time): if X → no Y
Premise 2: Every Z from Thing A's last year was Y.
  For Thing A (last year): if Z → yes Y
Conclusion: Thing A last year didn't have any Z's that were X
  For Thing A (last year): if Z → not X
```
Since Carriage Books is the common ingredient to all three claims, I would focus more on the moving parts.
```
Nonfiction is never profitable.   N → ~P
Last yr's books were profitable.  Last yr = P
So, last yr's books were fiction. Last yr = ~N
```
